w:r.w:t: GitHub Actions + Amazon S3 + AWS CodeDeploy + EC2 + PM2

PulseDesk is a fast-growing B2B SaaS company that provides a customer support and helpdesk platform for small-to-medium businesses. The platform supports support tickets, live chat, knowledge bases and customer satisfaction surveys. In the assessment scenario, PulseDesk serves over 4,000 business clients and processes roughly 2 million support interactions per month. The company’s technology stack includes a React/Next.js frontend, Node.js/Express backend microservices, PostgreSQL on RDS, Redis for caching, and AWS infrastructure services including EC2, RDS, S3 and VPC.

The problem described in the assessment brief is that PulseDesk releases features every two weeks, but its deployment process is manual and fragile. Deployments are performed manually over SSH by a single DevOps engineer, there is no staging environment, bugs are frequently found by customers rather than automated tests, and a previous failed release caused four hours of downtime, resulting in customer churn and SLA breaches.

The aim of this project is to design and implement a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test and deployment activities for the PulseDesk Node.js application. The final implementation uses GitHub Actions for CI/CD orchestration, Amazon S3 for deployment artefact storage, AWS CodeDeploy for automated deployment, Amazon EC2 as the staging environment, and PM2 as the Node.js process manager. This replaces the manual SSH deployment model with an automated staging deployment process.

The aim of this project is to implement a cloud-based CI/CD pipeline that enables automated testing and automated deployment of the PulseDesk Node.js/Express application to an AWS staging environment.

The assessment requires an AWS-hosted architecture with isolated networking and separate public/private subnet tiers for web, application and database components. It also requires a CI/CD pipeline that integrates version control, automated testing, build automation, a CI server, and deployment to staging using AWS CodeDeploy with automated health checks and rollback on failure.
The implemented solution focuses on the CI/CD deployment path by using a working EC2 staging instance registered with AWS CodeDeploy.

The full target VPC architecture for PulseDesk include

This design satisfies the brief’s requirement for public/private subnet separation across web, app and database tiers.
The implemented demonstration uses a single EC2 staging instance to prove the CI/CD deployment path. A production-grade extension would move the application instance
into a private subnet behind an Application Load Balancer and use a database subnet group for RDS.

Although the implemented CI/CD pipeline does not require a live database, the PulseDesk scenario specifies PostgreSQL on Amazon RDS and Redis for caching. In a full production deployment, the database tier would be hosted in private subnets within the VPC, isolated from the public internet and accessible only from the application tier via security groups. RDS would provide automated backups, Multi
AZ failover, and managed patching. Application instances would retrieve database credentials securely from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store or Secrets Manager during deployment.

While the staging demonstration focuses on CI/CD deployment to EC2, the architecture is designed so that the same pipeline could deploy application updates that connect to a private RDS instance without modification. This satisfies the assessment requirement to consider database placement, security, and integration within the overall cloud infrastructure.

The assignment brief requires automated testing, build automation and CI triggering.

The implementation includes Jest-based automated testing as part of the GitHub Actions CI workflow. In addition, practical endpoint testing was conducted manually from the command line by remotely accessing the EC2 staging instance over SSH. This approach was adopted to keep testing focused while troubleshooting deployment issues and identifying API endpoint failures.

During deployment troubleshooting, command-line testing was valuable because it enabled the application to be tested directly within the EC2 environment where the CodeDeploy deployment was running. After connecting to the instance, terminal commands were used to inspect the deployed application directory, confirm whether PM2 was running the Node.js process, review CodeDeploy lifecycle logs, and test the application endpoint locally on the instance.

This test confirmed whether the Express application was running correctly on the EC2 instance and whether the
endpoint returned a successful response. It also aligned with the CodeDeploy
lifecycle hook, which used the same endpoint to verify deployment health before marking the deployment as successful.

Command-line testing was necessary because the initial deployment failures were not caused solely by application code. The issues included CodeDeploy agent credential problems, missing Node.js and npm on the EC2 instance, the absence of PM2 during the first deployment, and lifecycle script failures. Testing directly on the EC2 instance made it possible to identify where the deployment was failing and to confirm when each issue had been resolved.

In the final implementation, automated API testing was added using Postman and Newman. A dedicated Postman collection was created for the /health endpoint, and GitHub Actions executes this collection using Newman as part of the CI workflow. The Newman step validates that the deployed application responds with HTTP 200 and returns the expected "OK" message. This ensures that API-level validation occurs automatically during CI before deployment proceeds. While the Newman test suite currently focuses on the /health endpoint, it provides a foundation for expanding into broader API regression testing. This enhancement strengthens the automated testing requirement of the assessment and provides a more realistic CI/CD validation stage compared to manual curl-based checks alone.

During refinement, the Express application was separated into src/app.js and server.js. The src/app.js file defines and exports the Express application so that it can be tested directly by Jest/Supertest. The server.js file imports the same application and starts the
HTTP listener on port 3000 for the deployed EC2 environment. This avoids duplicate route definitions and ensures that the application tested in CI is the same application deployed by CodeDeploy.

Automatic rollback was configured on the PulseDeskStaging deployment group so that deployment failure can trigger rollback to the previous known-good application revision. This supports the assignment requirement that failed deployments roll back automatically.

AWS CodeDeploy was configured to support automatic rollback for the PulseDesk staging deployment group. Automatic rollback is important because it reduces the need for manual intervention when a deployment fails and helps return the staging environment to the last known good application revision.

CodeDeploy supports both automatic and manual rollback. AWS documentation states that a deployment group or individual deployment can be configured to automatically roll back when a deployment fails or when a specified monitoring threshold is met. In this case, CodeDeploy deploys the last known good application revision. AWS also notes that rolled-back deployments are technically new deployments with new deployment IDs, rather than restored versions of a previous deployment.

For the PulseDesk staging environment, the key rollback trigger is deployment failure. This means that if a lifecycle hook fails, if an instance fails validation, or if the /health endpoint does not respond successfully during the ValidateService lifecycle event,
CodeDeploy marks the deployment as failed and can roll back to the previous successful revision. This aligns with the project’s use of ValidateService, where the deployment runs:
If this health check fails, the deployment does not complete successfully.

From an infrastructure-as-code perspective, AWS documents that CodeDeploy automatic rollback configuration includes an Enabled property and rollback Events. The documented rollback event values include DEPLOYMENT_FAILURE, DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM, and DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_REQUEST. For this project, the most relevant rollback event is DEPLOYMENT_FAILURE.

If deployment fails, CodeDeploy automatically redeploys the previous known-good revision

This rollback configuration strengthens the deployment strategy because it addresses the original PulseDesk problem of slow manual rollbacks. In the company brief, PulseDesk previously required manual rollback intervention that took over an hour after a failed release. The implemented CodeDeploy rollback approach reduces this risk by allowing failed deployments to be automatically reverted through the deployment group configuration

During implementation, the CodeDeploy agent initially failed with missing credentials. The issue was resolved by ensuring the EC2 instance had the correct IAM instance profile and restarting the CodeDeploy agent so it could read the instance profile credentials.
This was an important operational lesson: changes to an EC2 instance role may require restarting the CodeDeploy agent or the instance before the agent correctly picks up the new credentials.

Store SSH keys outside the repository directory.
Avoid committing credentials or deployment secrets.
Use GitHub Actions secrets and IAM roles instead of hard-coded credentials.

SSH access should remain restricted to the developer’s trusted public IP address. Port 3000 is acceptable for controlled staging testing, but a production-like environment should use an Application Load Balancer or Nginx reverse proxy on ports 80 and 443, rather than exposing the Node.js application port directly.

The S3 bucket containing deployment artefacts should remain private. Access should be limited to the GitHub Actions deployment role and the EC2/CodeDeploy role required to retrieve deployment bundles.

AWS CodePipeline was considered as a possible orchestration tool. It integrates well with AWS services such as CodeBuild, S3 and CodeDeploy. GitHub Actions was selected because the repository is hosted in GitHub, the workflow is easy to demonstrate, and pipeline status is visible directly from the repository.
The final design still uses AWS-native deployment through CodeDeploy, so the solution combines GitHub-native CI/CD orchestration with AWS-native EC2 deployment.

Containers were considered as a future option. A Docker-based approach could package the application runtime and reduce dependency installation work on EC2. However, EC2 was chosen because the assessment scenario specifically asks for AWS CodeDeploy deployment to a staging EC2 environment.
The initial build simulated a staging deployment using GitHub Actions Environments because access to AWS EC2 resources was not yet available.

That approach was useful during the early design phase, but it has now been replaced by a real AWS CodeDeploy deployment to EC2. The final implementation is stronger because it demonstrates an actual cloud-hosted staging deployment.

This project delivered a working CI/CD pipeline for the PulseDesk Node.js application. GitHub Actions provides automated CI and deployment orchestration, Amazon S3 stores the deployment bundle, and AWS CodeDeploy deploys the application to a staging EC2 environment using AppSpec lifecycle hooks.
The final implementation demonstrated a successful deployment in which Node.js and npm were installed, application dependencies were configured, PM2 was installed, the application was started as
validation check passed. AWS CodeDeploy reported the deployment as successful, with one of one instances updated in the initial staging configuration.
The deployment group was also configured for automatic rollback on deployment failure, meaning that if a lifecycle event or health check fails, CodeDeploy can redeploy
the previous known-good revision. This directly addresses the PulseDesk requirement for faster recovery from failed releases.
Overall, the report demonstrates that a code change pushed to the

branch can trigger the automated pipeline and update the staging environment without manual SSH deployment steps. This directly addresses the original PulseDesk problem of manual releases, the absence of a staging environment, and slow deployment recovery.

Automated API validation using Newman further strengthened the reliability of the CI stage by ensuring the application responded correctly before deployment.
